text: Patent claims define the legal boundaries of the invention — what the patent owner can exclude others from making, using, selling. Claims are the most important part of a patent; the specification supports and explains the claims. Types: Independent claims (standalone, define complete invention), Dependent claims (refer back to and narrow an independent claim). For AYUSH patents, claims typically cover: composition/formulation, process of making, method of treatment/use, dosage form. Well-drafted claims balance breadth (maximizing protection) with validity (surviving prior art challenges).

Independent claim: 'A pharmaceutical composition comprising: 5-10% w/w extract of Withania somnifera, 2-5% w/w extract of Bacopa monnieri, and a pharmaceutically acceptable carrier.' Dependent claim: 'The composition of claim 1, wherein the carrier is selected from lactose, starch, or microcrystalline cellulose.' Strategy: Independent claims should be as broad as possible while still novel/inventive. Dependent claims add specific embodiments — if independent is invalidated, dependent may survive. For AYUSH: have claims at different specificity levels.

Common claim categories for AYUSH patents: 1) Composition claims — 'A formulation comprising X, Y, Z in specific ratios'. 2) Process claims — 'A process for preparing extract comprising steps a, b, c'. 3) Method of treatment claims — 'A method for treating diabetes comprising administering composition X' (Note: not patentable in India under Section 3(i)). 4) Use claims — 'Use of composition X for the manufacture of a medicament for treating Y' (Swiss-type claim, limited acceptance). 5) Product-by-process claims — 'An extract obtained by the process of claim 5'. 6) Kit claims — 'A kit comprising formulation X and applicator Y'.

Section 3(i) of Patents Act 1970 excludes 'any process for the medicinal, surgical, curative, prophylactic, diagnostic, therapeutic or other treatment of human beings or animals'. This means method of treatment claims are NOT patentable in India. Workaround: Use 'Swiss-type' claims — 'Use of compound X for the manufacture of a medicament for treating condition Y'. This claims the use in manufacturing, not the treatment itself. For AYUSH: focus on composition and process claims rather than method of treatment claims.

Best practices for AYUSH patent claims: 1) Use clear, precise language — avoid ambiguity. 2) Define key terms in specification — what is 'extract', 'effective amount'. 3) Use ranges rather than single values — '5-15% w/w' not 'exactly 10%'. 4) Include alternatives — 'selected from the group consisting of A, B, C'. 5) Claim both genus (broad) and species (specific). 6) Support every claim element in specification. 7) Avoid unnecessary limitations — each word narrows scope. 8) Use proper claim format — preamble, transitional phrase, body. 9) Review for Section 3(d) compliance — ensure claims reflect enhanced efficacy.

Claim structure: PREAMBLE — introduces the invention type ('A pharmaceutical composition', 'A process for preparing'). TRANSITIONAL PHRASE — connects preamble to body. Key phrases: 'comprising' (open-ended, allows additional elements), 'consisting of' (closed, only listed elements), 'consisting essentially of' (allows minor additions not affecting basic characteristics). BODY — lists the elements/steps of the invention. For AYUSH: use 'comprising' for formulations (allows additional excipients), 'consisting of' only when you want to exclude additional actives.

Means-plus-function claims recite a 'means for' performing a function rather than specific structure. Example: 'means for heating' instead of 'a heater'. In India, such claims are interpreted to cover the specific structure described in the specification and equivalents. Advantage: broader coverage. Disadvantage: may be indefinite if specification doesn't describe structure. For AYUSH process claims: avoid means-plus-function; describe actual equipment/steps for clarity.

Markush claims define a group of alternatives: 'A compound selected from the group consisting of A, B, C, and D'. Named after Ex parte Markush (US decision). Useful when several compounds/ingredients have same function. For AYUSH formulations: 'A composition comprising an adaptogen selected from the group consisting of Withania somnifera, Rhodiola rosea, Eleutherococcus senticosus, and Panax ginseng'. Limitation: all alternatives must share common property and meet unity of invention.

Product-by-process claims define a product by the process used to make it: 'An extract obtained by supercritical CO2 extraction of Curcuma longa at 40°C and 300 bar pressure'. Useful when: product is novel but hard to characterize structurally, or when process imparts special properties. Limitation: product must still be novel over prior art products regardless of how made. For AYUSH: use when extraction method creates unique composition that's hard to define chemically.

Claim differentiation doctrine: each claim is presumed to have different scope than others. If independent claim says 'an extract' and dependent says 'wherein the extract is aqueous', the independent covers non-aqueous too. Practical implication: don't repeat same limitations in dependent claims. Strategy for AYUSH: Independent claim — broad formulation. Dependent claims — specific ingredients, ratios, dosage forms, particle sizes, stability parameters. Each dependent adds value only if it adds a patentable distinction.

When claiming numerical ranges (concentration, temperature, pH), prior art may overlap. Patentability depends on: 1) Whether prior art teaches the specific range. 2) Whether applicant shows unexpected results at claimed range (criticality). 3) Whether range is narrow enough to avoid obviousness. For AYUSH: if prior art says '1-20% extract' and you claim '8-12%', show why 8-12% is critical (enhanced bioavailability, synergistic effect). Provide comparative data in specification supporting the range.

Negative limitations exclude elements: 'A composition substantially free of heavy metals', 'A formulation containing no synthetic preservatives'. Useful to distinguish from prior art that includes the excluded element. For AYUSH: if prior formulations contain a problematic ingredient (e.g., artificial colors), claim 'free of artificial colors' to differentiate. Caution: negative limitations can be hard to prove in infringement (how to show someone's product contains the excluded element?).

Omnibus claims (e.g., 'An invention as substantially described herein with reference to the examples') were previously allowed in India but are now discouraged/rejected. Modern practice requires specific, definite claims. For AYUSH: don't rely on omnibus claims. Draft specific claims covering: core formulation, preferred embodiments, processes, dosage forms. The specification can be broad, but claims must be definite.

Claims can be amended during prosecution to overcome objections, but amendments cannot add new matter or broaden scope. Allowable amendments: narrowing by adding limitations, clarifying ambiguous language, correcting errors, deleting claims. Not allowed: adding elements not in original specification, broadening numerical ranges, removing limitations. Strategy for AYUSH: file with broader claims, have fall-back positions ready in specification to narrow during prosecution if needed.

Claims must be: 1) Enabled — specification teaches how to make and use the full scope of claims without undue experimentation. 2) Supported by written description — specification shows inventor possessed the invention. For AYUSH: if claiming 'extracts of Withania somnifera', specification should describe extraction methods for various parts (root, leaf, whole plant) and various solvents. If claiming a range, provide examples across the range. Insufficient disclosure leads to Section 10 objection.
